notes.front: What is kubectl?
notes.back: The command-line tool for communicating with a Kubernetes cluster's control plane, using the Kubernetes API.
notes.explanation: Each kubectl command becomes HTTP requests to the API server, which validates them and applies them to the cluster state stored in etcd.
notes.example: kubectl get pods lists your Pods; kubectl logs shows what a container has written to its output.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “The kubectl command-line tool”; Kubernetes glossary, “Kubectl”

notes.front: What is a kubeconfig file?
notes.back: A file organising clusters, users, namespaces and authentication details, which kubectl uses to find and talk to a cluster's API server.
notes.explanation: The name is generic: any file used to configure cluster access is a kubeconfig file, not only one called kubeconfig.
notes.example: One kubeconfig holding a dev and a prod “context” (a saved cluster, user and namespace) lets you switch clusters without reconfiguring anything.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files”

notes.front: What are kubectl's object management techniques?
notes.back: Three ways to create and manage objects: imperative commands, imperative object configuration and declarative object configuration.
notes.explanation: Manage any one object with only one technique; mixing them for the same object gives undefined behaviour.
notes.example: kubectl create deployment nginx --image nginx is an imperative command; kubectl apply -f configs/ is declarative.

notes.front: What does kubectl apply do?
notes.back: Declarative management: it creates or updates live objects to match configuration files, working out the needed operation per object.
notes.explanation: It records the applied configuration in an annotation and changes only the fields your files set, so changes made to the live object by other tools are kept.
notes.example: Edit one file in configs/, run kubectl apply -f configs/, and only the object whose file changed is updated.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Configuration Files”

notes.front: What is Kustomize?
notes.back: A tool for customising Kubernetes configurations through a kustomization file; kubectl has supported it since 1.14.
notes.explanation: It can generate ConfigMaps and Secrets from files, add the same label or namespace to many objects at once, and combine several sets of manifests; kubectl apply -k applies the result.
notes.example: Generate a ConfigMap from an application.properties file instead of writing its YAML by hand.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize”

notes.front: What is a Helm chart?
notes.back: A package of pre-configured Kubernetes configurations that can be managed with the Helm tool.
notes.explanation: Charts give a reproducible way to create and share Kubernetes applications.
notes.example: One chart might deploy a single small cache Pod; another, a full web stack with HTTP servers, databases and caches.

notes.front: What is kubeadm?
notes.back: A tool for quickly installing Kubernetes and setting up a secure cluster.
notes.explanation: It installs both the control plane and the worker node components.
notes.example: Building a lab cluster on three of your own machines, rather than using a cloud provider's managed service.

notes.front: What are minikube and kOps for?
notes.back: minikube runs Kubernetes locally for learning; kOps creates, upgrades and maintains production clusters and provisions their cloud infrastructure.
notes.explanation: minikube runs an all-in-one or multi-node local cluster inside a VM on your computer.
notes.example: Practising for an exam on a laptop: minikube. Running highly available production clusters on AWS: kOps.

notes.front: What is a ResourceQuota?
notes.back: An object that limits the total resource consumption, and the number of objects, allowed in one namespace.
notes.explanation: It stops one team from using more than its fair share of a shared cluster; each team works in its own namespace with its own quota.
notes.example: Team A's namespace may use at most a fixed total of CPU and memory, and hold at most a set number of Pods.

notes.front: What is a LimitRange?
notes.back: A per-namespace policy that constrains the resources each Pod or container may ask for or use, and can set defaults.
notes.explanation: It stops a single object from monopolising a namespace's resources, whereas a ResourceQuota caps the namespace's total.
notes.example: Every container in namespace dev gets default CPU and memory values if it does not state its own.

notes.front: What does draining a node mean?
notes.back: Safely removing all Pods from a node to prepare it for maintenance or for removal from the cluster.
notes.explanation: kubectl drain marks the node as going out of service; it respects PodDisruptionBudgets and retries refused requests until done or timed out.
notes.example: Before patching a node's kernel, drain it: its Pods shut down gracefully and their controllers recreate them on other nodes.

notes.front: How often does Kubernetes publish a new minor release?
notes.back: Approximately three times per year.
notes.explanation: Versions are written x.y.z (major, minor, patch), following Semantic Versioning; a minor release is a change in y.
notes.example: 1.37.0 was released on 26 August 2026; the next minor is 1.38.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Which Kubernetes releases does the project maintain?
notes.back: Release branches for the three most recent minor releases; 1.19 and newer get about 1 year of patch support.
notes.explanation: Releases 1.18 and older received about 9 months; older releases get no security updates or bug fixes.
notes.example: With 1.37 the latest, the maintained minors are 1.37, 1.36 and 1.35.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: What does the Kubernetes version skew policy define?
notes.back: The supported differences in version between cluster components, measured against kube-apiserver.
notes.explanation: It tells you which kubelet and kubectl versions may run with a given API server, and in what order to upgrade.
notes.example: Like app versions that must stay compatible with a phone's operating system: a few versions behind is fine, ahead is not.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: What does the Kubernetes deprecation policy govern?
notes.back: How long API versions, flags and features must keep working after being deprecated, depending on their stability level.
notes.explanation: It gives users time to migrate; for API versions, the rules differ for alpha, beta and GA.
notes.example: Like a bus company promising to run an old route for a set time after announcing its replacement.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: What are the Kubernetes glossary's personas?
notes.back: Roles people play around Kubernetes, such as application developer or cluster operator.
notes.explanation: The four are application developer, cluster operator, cluster architect and platform developer.
notes.example: One person can hold several: a small team's developer may also keep its cluster running.
notes.source: Kubernetes glossary, “Application Developer”, “Cluster Operator”, “Cluster Architect”, “Platform Developer”

notes.front: Where does kubectl look for its kubeconfig by default?
notes.back: In a file named config in the $HOME/.kube directory.
notes.explanation: The KUBECONFIG environment variable or the --kubeconfig flag can point to other files.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files”

notes.front: In a kubeconfig, what three parameters does a context group together?
notes.back: A cluster, a namespace and a user.
notes.explanation: kubectl uses the current context's parameters to talk to the cluster; kubectl config use-context changes it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files”, “Context”

notes.front: If KUBECONFIG lists several files, which configuration does kubectl use?
notes.back: The result of merging all the listed files.
notes.explanation: The list is colon-separated on Linux and Mac, semicolon-separated on Windows.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files”, “The KUBECONFIG environment variable”

notes.front: Which technique operates directly on live objects, keeps no history of earlier configurations, and suits one-off tasks?
notes.back: Imperative commands.
notes.explanation: It has the lowest learning curve but gives no audit trail, change review or template for new objects.

notes.front: Which technique names an operation such as create or replace, plus at least one file holding a full object definition?
notes.back: Imperative object configuration.
notes.explanation: The replace command overwrites the whole spec, dropping changes that are not in the file.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Object Management”, “Imperative object configuration”

notes.front: Which technique works on directories of files and lets kubectl detect create, update and delete per object?
notes.back: Declarative object configuration.
notes.explanation: It keeps changes other writers made to live objects, but unexpected results are harder to debug.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Object Management”, “Declarative object configuration”

notes.front: Which kubectl apply flag applies the resources in a directory containing a kustomization file?
notes.back: --kustomize, or its short form -k.
notes.explanation: kubectl kustomize <directory> shows the resources without applying them.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize”

notes.front: How does kubeadm run kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler and etcd on control plane nodes?
notes.back: As static Pods.
notes.explanation: The kubelet on each control plane node supervises them directly and restarts them if they fail.

notes.front: What does the API server return when creating or updating an object would break a ResourceQuota?
notes.back: HTTP 403 Forbidden, with a message explaining which constraint would be violated.
notes.explanation: The request is rejected; nothing is created.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Resource Quotas”, “How Kubernetes ResourceQuotas work”

notes.front: Does lowering a ResourceQuota affect resources that were already created?
notes.back: No. Neither contention nor changes to a quota affect already created resources.
notes.explanation: Quota is checked when resources are created or updated.

notes.front: How far may the kubelet's version differ from kube-apiserver's?
notes.back: It must not be newer, and may be up to three minor versions older.
notes.explanation: kubelets older than 1.25 could only be up to two minor versions older.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: How far may kubectl's version differ from kube-apiserver's?
notes.back: Within one minor version, older or newer.
notes.explanation: In a highly available cluster with mixed API server versions, the supported kubectl range narrows.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: What should you do to a node before a minor-version kubelet upgrade?
notes.back: Drain its Pods first; in-place minor-version kubelet upgrades are not supported.
notes.explanation: kube-apiserver is upgraded first, because the kubelet must never be newer than it.
notes.source: Kubernetes, “Version Skew Policy”, “Supported component upgrade order”

notes.front: Under the deprecation policy, how soon must a beta API version be deprecated, and how long is it then still served?
notes.back: Deprecated within 9 months or 3 minor releases of appearing, then served for at least 9 months or 3 more; whichever is longer, each time.
notes.explanation: This makes beta support cover the maximum supported version skew, and stops APIs stagnating in beta.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Under the deprecation policy, when may a GA API version be removed, and when may an alpha one?
notes.back: GA: never within a major version. Alpha: in any release, without prior deprecation notice.
notes.explanation: There are no current plans for a major version of Kubernetes that removes GA APIs.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Your kubeconfig defines dev and prod contexts. Which kubectl command makes prod the one you work with?
notes.back: kubectl config use-context prod.
notes.explanation: kubectl then uses the cluster, namespace and user of that current context.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files”, “Context”

notes.front: kubectl create deployment nginx --image nginx: which object management technique is this?
notes.back: An imperative command.
notes.explanation: The operation and its details are given as arguments and flags, on live objects, with no configuration file.

notes.front: kubectl replace -f nginx.yaml: which object management technique is this?
notes.back: Imperative object configuration.
notes.explanation: The command names the operation (replace) and a file with the full object definition.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Object Management”, “Imperative object configuration”

notes.front: kubectl apply -f configs/: which object management technique is this?
notes.back: Declarative object configuration.
notes.explanation: kubectl works out per object whether to create, patch or delete; you do not name the operation.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Object Management”, “Declarative object configuration”

notes.front: A new version of Deployment web is failing. Which kubectl command rolls it back to the previous revision?
notes.back: kubectl rollout undo deployment/web.
notes.explanation: Add --to-revision=<n> to go back to a specific revision; kubectl rollout history lists them.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Deployments”, “Rolling Back to a Previous Revision”

notes.front: You want a small Kubernetes cluster on your laptop to practise. Which tool from the glossary fits?
notes.back: minikube.
notes.explanation: minikube runs Kubernetes locally, inside a VM on your computer; kOps targets production clusters in the cloud.

notes.front: You need to install Kubernetes yourself on three servers and set up a secure cluster. Which tool fits?
notes.back: kubeadm.
notes.explanation: kubeadm installs both the control plane and the worker node components.

notes.front: You want to share your application, made of many Kubernetes manifests, as one reproducible package others can install. What fits?
notes.back: A Helm chart.
notes.explanation: Charts package pre-configured Kubernetes configurations for creating and sharing applications.

notes.front: You want kubectl itself to generate a ConfigMap from a properties file and apply it together with your other manifests. Which feature fits?
notes.back: Kustomize (configMapGenerator, applied with kubectl apply -k).
notes.explanation: Kustomize is built into kubectl and can generate ConfigMaps and Secrets from files or literals.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize”

notes.front: A Deployment asks for more resources than its namespace's ResourceQuota allows. Is the Deployment created?
notes.back: Yes, but it may not be able to create all of its Pods.
notes.explanation: Check the Deployment's status, for example with kubectl describe, to see what happened.

notes.front: In a namespace with a LimitRange that sets defaults, a Pod is created without any compute resource settings. What happens?
notes.back: Kubernetes fills in the LimitRange’s default values for the Pod’s containers as the Pod is created.
notes.explanation: A LimitRange can also enforce minimum and maximum CPU and memory for each Pod or container in the namespace.

notes.front: A node needs a hardware repair. Which command safely empties it of Pods first, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets?
notes.back: kubectl drain <node>.
notes.explanation: kubectl drain removes the node's Pods through an API that honours PodDisruptionBudgets, retrying until done or timed out.

notes.front: The latest Kubernetes minor release is 1.37. Which minors have maintained release branches?
notes.back: 1.37, 1.36 and 1.35: the three most recent minors.
notes.explanation: An older minor can still get patches until its end-of-life date: on 25 September 2026 the Releases page gave 1.34's as 27 October 2026.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: About how many new Kubernetes minor versions should a platform team plan to upgrade through each year?
notes.back: About three.
notes.explanation: Minor releases come roughly three times a year, and each is patched for about a year.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: kube-apiserver runs 1.37. Which of these kubelet versions is supported: 1.38 or 1.34?
notes.back: 1.34. A kubelet may be up to three minors older, but never newer.
notes.explanation: 1.38 is newer than the API server, which the policy does not allow.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: kube-apiserver runs 1.37. Is kubectl 1.35 supported?
notes.back: No. kubectl must be within one minor version, so only 1.36, 1.37 or 1.38.
notes.explanation: The kubectl limit is stricter than the kubelet's three minors.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: A beta API version you rely on has just been deprecated. What is the minimum time it must still be served?
notes.back: 9 months or 3 minor releases, whichever is longer.
notes.explanation: After that it may stop being served, so migrate to the replacement version in that window.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Which persona writes an application that runs in a Kubernetes cluster?
notes.back: Application developer.
notes.explanation: Their focus is one part of an application, at whatever scale.

notes.front: Which persona configures, controls and monitors clusters and keeps them running, including upgrades?
notes.back: Cluster operator.
notes.explanation: This persona is different from the Operator pattern that extends the Kubernetes API.

notes.front: Which persona designs infrastructure involving one or more Kubernetes clusters, with an eye on high availability and security?
notes.back: Cluster architect.
notes.explanation: They are concerned with best practices for distributed systems.

notes.front: Which persona customises the Kubernetes platform itself, for example with custom resources, to fit a project?
notes.back: Platform developer.
notes.explanation: Some contribute such extensions to the community; others keep them in-house.

notes.front: How does a ResourceQuota differ from a LimitRange?
notes.back: ResourceQuota caps a namespace's total consumption and object counts; LimitRange constrains each Pod or container within it.
notes.explanation: They are often used together: the LimitRange can also supply defaults that the quota requires.

notes.front: Why is declarative object configuration preferred for production over imperative commands?
notes.back: Its files can live in version control and go through review and audit; imperative commands leave no record beyond the live state.
notes.explanation: Imperative commands remain the easiest way to get started or run a one-off task.

notes.front: How do Kustomize and Helm charts differ in how they are used with Kubernetes?
notes.back: Kustomize customises configuration through a kustomization file and is built into kubectl; a Helm chart is a package managed with the separate Helm tool.
notes.explanation: Both help manage sets of manifests; charts focus on packaging and sharing applications.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize”; Kubernetes glossary, “Helm Chart”
